title: Scipio's dream
hookLine: in Cicero's Dream of Scipio, Rome looks tiny from the stars and fame is short (Republic 6)

lines: YEAR ONE: A SPECK IN A SUNBEAM.
A GENERAL LIFTED TO THE STARS.
cards: Back in year one, this path spent a day with the pale blue dot, the 1990 photo in which Earth is a speck in a sunbeam. The photo was new. The feeling it gives is not.

Everything people fight over, smaller than a grain of dust: about two thousand years before that spacecraft, Cicero wrote it as a dream, in which a young Roman general is lifted among the stars and looks back at his empire.

teach.h: THE DREAM AT THE END OF A LOST BOOK.
teach.b: First, the frame. Cicero's book On the Republic ends with a dream told by Scipio Aemilianus, the general whose circle Panaetius joined.
Most of that book was lost for centuries, but the dream survived on its own, because a later writer, Macrobius, wrote a long commentary on it. Second, the dream.

teach.h: FROM THE STARS, ROME IS A POINT.
teach.b: Scipio falls asleep and meets his well-known grandfather by adoption, Scipio Africanus, the conqueror of Hannibal, who lifts him high among the stars.
Looking down, Scipio finds the earth so small that the Roman Empire, which he's spent his life serving, seems a tiny point. He's almost ashamed of it. Third, the lesson about fame.

teach.h: FAME CAN'T REACH FAR OR LAST.
teach.b: Africanus tells him plainly: your name can't reach most of the earth, much less last. People in other regions will never hear of you; people in later ages will forget.
Even the long ages of the sky make human fame seem brief. So don't work for glory. Fourth, what to do instead, and Stoic readers will recognize it.
The dream doesn't say: nothing matters, so do nothing.
It says: serve your country well, care for its people, and your reward isn't fame but something higher. In the dream, those who serve well find a place in the heavens.
Readers take that differently: some literally, some as poetry.
Either way, the view from the stars isn't meant to shrink your effort. It shrinks your need for applause, and leaves the work.

how: Some readers use the Dream of Scipio as an exercise of the imagination, picturing the earth from the stars to loosen the hold of fame, then returning to their work.

o: a prophecy that Rome would rule the whole earth
a nightmare Africanus had before facing Hannibal
a vision of Rome tiny from the stars, fame brief

p: his commentary kept the dream alive
a tiny point from the stars

s: Cicero's whole Republic survived through the Middle Ages
most of it was lost; the dream survived through Macrobius's commentary.
in the dream, Africanus says fame can't reach far or last long
other regions won't hear of you, and later ages will forget.
the dream concludes that since Rome is tiny, public service doesn't matter
it urges Scipio to serve well, for a reward higher than fame.

games.q: you're Scipio, floating among the stars, and your empire looks like a dot. what does Africanus tell you to do?
o: give up public life; none of it matters.
serve your country well, without working for fame.
work harder so your name reaches farther.
games.why: the view from the stars shrinks the need for glory, not the duty. Africanus urges service, with a reward higher than fame.

practice: Close your eyes, if you like, and go straight to Scipio's height, among the stars, the earth a small bright point below. Bring to mind one thing you've wanted credit for lately, and ask how far word of it travels: a room, a street?
Notice what's left when the applause is too small to see: the work itself, and the people it helped. Then come back down, into the room.

wordCard.voice: Scipio's dream. In Cicero's dream story, Rome looks tiny from the stars, and fame is short, so serve well without needing the applause. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: a dream. Somnium Scipionis, the Dream of Scipio, closes Cicero's On the Republic.

carryVoice: Your line: from the stars. Seen from up there, all of Rome is a point. That's day six hundred forty-seven.
